newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Wharf's 1996 profits below expectations.
newsitem.headline: Wharf's 1996 profits below expectations.

text.p: Net profit growth at Wharf (Holdings) Ltd came in below expectations with the Hong Kong conglomerate posting a 24 percent decline in 1996 net profit, prompting analysts to lower their forecasts for its 1997 profit.
The group announced on Friday a net profit of HK$2.74 billion (US$354 million) in 1996 against 1995's HK$3.60 billion.
Analysts knew Wharf would not match 1995, which was boosted by a HK$1.51 billion exceptional gain, but expectations had averaged around HK$3.23 billion.
"I am mildly disappointed," said DBS Securities analyst Philip Tulk.

The discrepancy was due to an above-forecast loss from Wharf's wholly-owned cable television unit Wharf Cable Ltd, and below-expectation income from property sales and rental income, said analysts who attended a briefing hosted by the company.
"Cable was quoted some time ago in the Chinese press as indicating that they are putting out a loss of something like HK$400 million," Tulk said. "The operating loss was HK$580 million."
HSBC James Capel analyst Vincent Luk said he had forecast Cable's operating loss at HK$450 million for 1996. The unit booked a loss of HK$824 million in 1995.
Luk said rental income, which turned out to be HK$2.7 billion, fell short of his expectation at HK$3 billion.
Wharf said operating profit from its core investment properties, Harbour City and Times Square, rose 7.6 percent.
Tulk noted property sales income was also under expectation.
"The property sales numbers were lower than forecast. They booked HK$300 million in property sales," he said, adding he had anticipated HK$400 million.
Wharf said income from property sales was higher than in the previous year but did not elaborate.
In light of the 1996 results, Tulk said he was likely to revise his 1997 earnings forecast slightly downward by about HK$100 million from the original HK$3.77 billion.
The adjustment would be small as the negative impact from Cable would be moderated by the booking of property sales originally tipped to be recorded in 1996, Tulk said.
He noted the company was tied up in low-yield office and retail properties in Hong Kong.
"Their capital value has gone up very strongly but rents are not going up," he said, adding rents would fall for the group's investment properties in some areas this year.
Luk said he would revise his 1997 earnings forecast for the group because its rental income growth was not expected to be strong this year, but had yet to work out a revised figure.
Wharf said in a statement its 1996 recurrent profit before exceptionals rose 25.4 percent to HK$2.63 billion, and the group was upbeat about its prospects.

"Given the strong fundamentals of our group's quality investments and recurrent earnings base, prospects remain positive for our core assets and new businesses," chairman and chief executive Gonzaga Li said in the statement.

"Contribution from property sales in the year ahead is expected to receive a significant boost when approval for the marketing of Diamond Hill's five residential towers, with a gross floor area of more than 1.1 million square feet, is obtained," the statement said.
Wharf holds 33.3 percent of the project.
